answers.justification: The rise coincides with the pilot (E1, E2), and June was already up on paper forms before the app went live. However, the change in recording (C9, C13), the lack of before-and-after call-bell data (C6), conflicting staff accounts (E3) and a non-signal on the control chart (C2) mean the pilot effect is neither established nor ruled out.

Several things point to better recording: no-harm and found-on-floor falls rose most (C9), the Q2 handover notes show unreported falls (C9), and staff say they now log more (C13, E3). But the June rise came before the app went live (E2, C9), harmed falls also rose slightly, and the app's own miss rate is unknown (C9). So 'mainly' is not established.

C5 shows few admissions and fewer from discharge-to-assess beds at Ashby Fold, flat occupancy and dependency, and 27 of the 31 Q3 falls by long-stay residents. This contradicts the manager's claim in E5.

Both homes stay inside their control limits, and similar rises have reverted before (C2). But C2 warns that a real 40% rise would take two to three quarters to show, so the chart cannot confirm that nothing changed.

Per C5, the GP reviews mostly stopped or reduced medicines, the one hypnotic started went to a resident with no recorded fall, and psychotropic and hypnotic use was flat. This counts against the manager's claim in E5.
The pilot coincides in time and place with the rise: only the pilot homes went red (E2). But the app switch at the same homes is an uncontrolled rival (C9, C4), so causation is not established.

Recorded falls rose with the app switch, there is a plausible mechanism and some evidence of under-reporting on paper (C9, C13). But the June rise came first and the pilot is a concurrent rival (E2), so causation is not shown.
C5 shows no shift toward frailer admissions: discharge-to-assess admissions fell, dependency was flat, and most falls were by long-stay residents.

No pre-pilot response times exist at Ashby Fold and Penmor Lodge records no answer times at all (C6). Staff accounts conflict (E3), and a slow-bell complaint was made in May, before the pilot (C11). So even an association cannot be shown.
Reverting would be justified if H1 were confirmed. But no pause criterion has been met (C7), the rise is confounded with the app switch (C9), and it is not a control-chart signal (C2).

A2 keeps the agreed safeguards (C7), corrects the dashboard's raw-count and reporting-method flaws (E2, C2, C9), fills the call-bell data gap (C6), and sets a dated decision point with Q4 data, which C2 says is needed to detect a real rise.

Nothing points to individual fault: training compliance is in date (C8), and better recording may itself explain the rise (C9, C13). Disciplining staff would punish the wrong party and discourage reporting.

The app raised completion of post-fall observations from 67% to 94% and caught a head injury (C12), and it captures falls that paper missed (C9). Withdrawing it would disable a protective control and suppress information.

The catalogue cannot separate the pilot effect from the recording change or chance (C2, C6, C9). The evidence therefore cannot support committing to a substantive decision now, either to revert or to proceed with rollout. A2's dated review exists for exactly that reason.

ambiguousItems: Q02: 'supported' is defensible. Unreported falls in the Q2 handover notes (3 clear and 3 ambiguous in 6 of 13 weeks, roughly 6-13 over the quarter if extrapolated), together with the rise concentrated in no-harm and found-on-floor falls, could account for most of the +15. Against that, the June paper-era rise and the rise in harmed falls argue for 'unknown'.

Q07: 'causal' is arguable, because there is a mechanism (paper forms took 20 minutes, so small falls went in the handover book) plus covariation plus direct evidence of Q2 under-reporting. But the pilot is a concurrent rival that has not been excluded.

Q14: it depends on whether A2 (continue the pilot plus a review) counts as a substantive decision. If keeping the pilot under its existing safeguards is treated as a substantive choice, 'sufficient' is defensible because it follows the pre-agreed protocol (C7).
Q06: 'unknown' is arguable if the confounded co-occurrence is not treated as showing an association attributable to the pilot.
caseProblems: E2/C9: the combined June count (7) already rose before the 1 July app go-live, on paper forms. This is a useful discriminating clue, but answer keys should check that it is intended, since it cuts against H2's 'mainly' claim.
C9 includes the phrase 'which were chosen to give the rota pilot better night data'. This openly explains why the two interventions were confounded, which is realistic but makes the confound salient.
C13: the operations team (aligned with the Director of Operations) helped draft the union survey questions. This is a deliberate bias marker that is fine, but worth noting.
C4: the vendor says the app rollout to the remaining homes is January 2027, consistent with C9. The pilot rota rollout is March 2027. No inconsistency, but readers could confuse the two rollouts.
Numeric checks pass: monthly, quarterly, time-of-day and harm-level totals reconcile (16 and 31), and the C2 rates match the occupancy figures in C5. No inconsistencies found.
No catalogue title leaks an answer outright. C12's title and content strongly signal that A4 is harmful, which is appropriate.

rulings.explanation: H2 claims the rise is *mainly* due to recording, so the answer depends on whether recording explains more than about 7.5 of the 15 extra falls. Scaling up C9's cross-check gives about 6.5 missed Q2 falls from the 3 clear entries and about 13 if the 3 ambiguous ones count. The range straddles half, which is the key's case for 'unknown'. The key's rationale leaves out evidence that tips the balance towards 'supported', though. The cross-check covered only night handover notes, yet day falls also rose (8 to 13, E4) while day staffing stayed the same. The pilot cannot explain that rise, but a recording change can. Most of the increase is in no-harm falls (10 to 22) and found-on-floor falls (5 to 14). The July step coincides with app go-live. In C13, 8 of 14 night staff say they now log falls they would not have written up on paper. Under the relative definition ('supports the claim more than its rivals'), H2 arguably beats H1 and H4. The counter-evidence is weak and rests on small numbers: harmed falls rose 6 to 9, and June (still on paper) had 7 falls. So 'unknown' and 'supported' can both be defended.
rulings.fix: In C9, change the cross-check to '2 entries clearly describe an unreported fall, and 3 more are ambiguous' (scaled up, about 4-11 against a rise of 15). Add: 'Day handover notes for the same six weeks were also checked and showed no unreported falls.' Recording then plausibly explains well under half of the rise, and the day-fall rise no longer points to it, so only 'unknown' is defensible.

rulings.explanation: R2 claims only that the app switch increased *recorded* counts, not that it explains most of the rise. Several pieces of evidence support a causal contribution. The July rise follows go-live on 1 July. The mechanism is plausible: paper forms took 20 minutes, so small falls went in the handover book (C13). C9's cross-check shows directly that paper missed falls in Q2. In C13, 8 of 14 staff report at individual level that they now log falls they would not have recorded on paper. That is close to a direct counterfactual, and it comes from a survey drafted with the operations team, which favoured blaming the rota, so it makes the testimony more credible rather than less. The pilot is a rival explanation for the *total* rise, but it cannot explain why the same kind of fall now gets recorded when it previously did not. The key's point that 'no Q3 check is possible' is real but is partly answered by the C13 logging question. 'Causal' and 'association-only' can both be defended.
rulings.fix: In C13, remove the question 'Do you now log incidents you would not have written up on paper?' with its results, and remove the free-text quote 'paper forms took 20 minutes, so the little ones went in the handover book'. That leaves no direct evidence that the app records falls paper would have missed, so only 'association-only' is defensible.

rulings.explanation: The highest-ranked action is A2. Part of A2 is evidence-gathering: rates on the control chart, call-bell sampling and a dated review. But A2 also commits the board to a substantive choice in answer to the question actually put to it: do not reverse the pilot now, and keep running it under its existing pause rules. The SUFF definition says that concluding no intervention is warranted counts as substantive. Keeping the status quo under a pre-agreed protocol (C7) whose pause criteria have not been met can reasonably be read as that kind of decision. On that reading the evidence is sufficient, because continuing a time-limited, safeguarded trial does not require proof that it is safe. The key's reading, that A2 is essentially deferral and therefore evidence-gathering, is also reasonable. The item definition does not settle which reading applies.
rulings.fix: Add to the SUFF definition: 'Continuing an existing arrangement under its current safeguards while gathering data for a later decision counts as evidence-gathering, not as a substantive decision.' Only 'insufficient' is then defensible.

rulings.explanation: Under the stated semantics, 'association-only' means the two conditions co-occur or correlate but causation is not established. 'Unknown' is reserved for evidence too thin to show even an association. Here the pilot and the higher recorded counts do co-occur: only at the two pilot homes, starting from June, with June already at 7 against 4-5 in April and May. The other seven homes had no comparable rise. Confounding by the app change stops the link being called causal, but it does not erase the observed co-occurrence. The definition does not require the association to be attributable to the pilot. Nothing in the evidence counts against the link. So 'association-only' is the only answer that fits the definitions.
